title: Proof pages for a consumer brand
metaTitle: Proof pages that return to the product
excerpt: A brand proof page should show a constraint, the decision, and the object clearly, then send a similar shopper to the product. Mood without a choice is decoration.
alt: Yellow California poppies against a clear blue sky. A single subject, plainly lit, which is how a product proof should read.
caption: Yellow California poppies against a clear blue sky. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a product proof page open with?
faqs.answer: Open with the constraint that made the previous version fail a customer, such as cloth that pilled, a refill that did not seat, or a heel that hurt on a long day. A manifesto in sentence one assumes the reader already agrees with you.

faqs.question: What counts as evidence?
faqs.answer: The object that resulted, photographed so the change is visible, with a caption that states the fact. A campaign still in fog is atmosphere. A press-logo grid is not the decision. A quote helps only when it describes the change and the customer agreed to be named.

faqs.question: How should the page end?
faqs.answer: End on the live product, in the shop's name, with the limit and the timing. If the proof describes a version you no longer sell, mark it as history. A story whose object is missing from the shop empties the trust it just built.

markdown:
A consumer brand case study page should show a constraint, the decision you made, and the object, clearly. Screenshots of a campaign, or a montage of mood, are decoration until the choice is visible. Close by showing how a similar shopper can see the product.

One decision, told plainly, helps a stranger who does not know you yet. They borrow your last hard choice as evidence that the object in the shop is the result of judgment, not of a theme.

## Start from the constraint

Name the limit in the first screen. The first cloth pilled. The bottle was sturdy and then thrown away. The popular color varied so much that returns climbed. A heel looked right and hurt on a long day. A constraint is a fact that made the previous version fail a customer.

Write who was stuck and what you refused to keep shipping. Two or three sentences. A reader who has met that failure in someone else's product will stay. A reader who meets a manifesto in sentence one will assume the page is for people who already agree with you.

Google's notes on [helpful content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) describe a useful "how": what was tested, what the evidence was, how the work was done. A product proof page can do that without pretending to be a laboratory. You wore the heel for a month. You ran the glaze to a temperature that stopped the worst warping. You stopped the color that you could not repeat. Process can be ordinary. Ordinary process is credible. A fake crisis is not. If the constraint was mild, say so.

Avoid a villain. You do not need to attack other brands to explain your own change. The constraint was inside your product. Keep it there. Shoppers who do not know you yet have no appetite for a feud. They have an appetite for a thing that works.

## The decision, including the cost

Show the choice. You could have described the pilling as character. You changed the cloth, accepted a heavier hand, and rephotographed the jacket. You could have sold the bottle as a one-time object. You priced a refill and redesigned the cap so the refill actually seats. The decision includes what you gave up. The lighter cloth. The simpler cap. A color people asked for and you could not make twice.

Mention the cost in a sentence. Heavier cloth costs more to ship. A refill program means you still support the first version of the bottle. A shopper hears responsibility in that sentence. A page that only publishes the happy object sounds like an advertisement. Advertisements are fine in their place. A proof page that admits a tradeoff sounds like a brand that will still be here when the sole wears down.

Be specific enough that the current product is recognizable. "We pursued excellence" is not a decision. "The jacket is now the heavier twill, and the lighter one is discontinued" is a decision. Link the live product. If the proof describes a version you no longer sell, mark it as history or the reader will try to buy a ghost. Nothing empties trust faster than a story whose object is missing from the shop.

Name the person who made the call if the about page has already introduced them. The proof and the people should agree. A decision with no owner feels like marketing wrote it. A decision with an owner feels like a workshop.

## The object, clearly, as the evidence

The evidence is the thing that resulted. Photograph it so a stranger can see what changed. The new twill, close enough to read the weight, with the previous cloth only if the comparison is honest and you still have a sample. The refill seated in the bottle. The heel, with a note on the last you changed. A campaign still of a model in fog is not evidence. It is the manifesto again.

Caption the fact. "Heavier twill, current jacket, same pattern as last year." The caption is part of the proof. A poetic caption throws away the comparison you took the picture to make. If you have a simple before-and-after, use it only when both images are yours and the conditions are fair. Different light, different crop, and a flattering angle on the new one is a trick. Tricks age badly on a page that asks for trust.

Then write how a similar shopper sees the product now. The link, the name, the price shape in one line, the limit they should expect. Variation in glaze. A four-week make time. A sole that is stiff until the second week. The reader should be able to decide, not only to admire.

Down the Cove, a public Hanabi project, is an ecommerce migration and redesign. The proof-page lesson from shop work of that kind is that the object and the catalog have to survive the story. A case study that never returns to the product is a studio talking to itself. Wabisabi's calm is a reminder that the photograph can be quiet and still be specific. Use references as standards. Do not invent results for them.

## What is not proof

A grid of press logos is not the constraint or the decision. A quote that says "obsessed" is not evidence. A video of the workshop with no narration of the choice is atmosphere. You may use one of these late, small, and only if it is true. None of them can lead.

Do not invent numbers. If returns of a color dropped, and you will stand by the figure, you may say so. If you only remember that returns "felt" lower, say you stopped the color because you could not repeat it. The second sentence is stronger than a theatrical percentage. This page will not supply a percentage you did not measure.

Screenshots of the website itself prove that a website exists. Include one only if the decision was about the shop: you moved the refill onto the same page as the bottle so people stopped buying the wrong thing. Crop to the change. Leave the browser chrome out. The reader is already on the site.

Testimonials, if you have permission, should describe the decision. "The new sole is stiffer, and it is the one I walk in." That helps the next shopper. "Best purchase ever" helps no one choose a size. Skip it.

## End on the product

The last section is the door. See the product. Use the name the shop uses. Repeat the limit. If there are two versions, say which one this proof describes and link both only if both are for sale. A proof page that ends on "the journey continues" drops the reader at the moment they were ready to look.

Offer the closest live fact. In stock, or made in four weeks. The sizes you actually have. The refill that fits this bottle and not the older one. Precision here is kindness. A shopper who orders the wrong refill because the story was dreamy will blame the brand, and they will be right.

A single question path is enough for the case the page cannot cover. A repair of a version you no longer photograph. Give one contact, and say who reads it. The primary action remains the product. Ten fields between the story and the object undo the clarity you just earned.

If you publish several proof pages, give each a distinct constraint. Cloth. Refill. Fit. Three pages that all say "we care about quality" will be skimmed as one. Put the constraint in the title. "Why the jacket is a heavier twill" is a title a shopper can use.

## Keep it maintainable

Write so a product editor can update the link and the photograph when the next batch changes the surface. One column, a few honest pictures, a clear link. Avoid a layout that requires a new campaign shoot for a small material change. A clear picture on the usual ground is better evidence than a mood you cannot repeat.

Link the proof from the product it changed, not only from a journal index. A story nobody can reach from the jacket page is a diary. The shopper on the jacket page is the person who needed it.

Hanabi's practice with proof is the same shape. Constraint, decision, and the work you can look at, told so a similar buyer can see themselves. For a consumer brand, that buyer is a shopper who does not know you yet. The work they need to see is the object.

Put the date of the decision on the page. A proof that reads as if it happened in an undated always will be quoted after the product has changed again. "Changed in March 2026" is a small line, and it tells the next editor when the story needs a check. Undated certainty is how a true decision becomes a stale advertisement.

## After the story, the labels

A reader who believes the story will try to move. The menu they meet should use the words the story just taught: the jacket, the refill, the repair. Navigation is that map. It is [navigation for a consumer brand](/blog/navigation-for-a-consumer-brand).

If you are choosing which decision deserves a page, start from [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring one real constraint, and the product it changed.
